judgments.catchwords: 1 . Before a matter proceeds to trial, parties must have a proper understanding of each other's respective cases as pleaded. The law permits a party to seek further and better particulars where necessary to clarify the opposing party's pleaded case. 2. In the present action founded on medical negligence, the 1st to 4th Defendants have filed the application in Enclosure 32 seeking further and better particulars of the Plaintiffs case. The application falls to be determined in accordance with the established principles governing such applications. 3. The overriding issue is whether the particulars sought by the 1st to 4th Defendants are necessary to clarify the material facts underlying the Plaintiffs pleaded case, or whether they go beyond that purpose by seeking details of the evidence by which the Plaintiff intends to prove her case. 4. This requires the Court to consider the nature and scope of each request in Enclosure 32, having regard to the Plaintiffs pleadings and the purpose for which the particulars are sought.

judgments.title: Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Berhad v Ang Eng Hooi & ors
judgments.catchwords: (1) in a unilateral and written undertaking given by one party, X (X’s Unilateral Undertaking), to another party (Y) with regard to a debt settlement agreement between Y and Z (Settlement Agreement) - (a) is X’s Unilateral Undertaking valid or void? In this regard, whether the Contracts Act 1950 (CA) applies to X’s Unilateral Undertaking. If the CA applies to X’s Unilateral Undertaking, was there “consideration” for X’s Unilateral Undertaking as understood in s 2(d) CA?; and (b) if X’s Unilateral Undertaking was valid - (i) whether ss 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act 1950 (EA) bar the admissibility of extrinsic evidence to contradict, vary, add to or subtract from the contents of X’s Unilateral Undertaking; and (ii) how should the court construe and enforce the contents of X’s Unilateral Undertaking?; and (2) upon a court’s removal of a private caveat over a piece of land, whether the registered proprietor of the land (Land Owner) can claim compensation from the caveator under s 329(1) of the National Land Code (NLC) for - (a) all legal fees incurred by the Land Owner to apply to court for the removal of the private caveat; (b) the higher interest rate imposed by a lender on the Land Owner allegedly due to the entry of the private caveat; (c) the higher construction cost incurred by the Land Owner with regard to the Land Owner’s construction of a building on the land, purportedly as a result of the entry of the private caveat; and (d) loss of potential business suffered by the Land Owner allegedly due to the entry of the private caveat.
coram: YA Datuk Wong Kian Kheong
YA Dato' Dr Alwi Bin Abdul Wahab
YA Dato' Ahmad Kamal Bin Md. Shahid

judgments.catchwords: Criminal Law—Murder—Child victim—Mens rea—Accused stepfather charged under s 302 of the Penal Code for causing death of two-year-and-seven-month-old stepdaughter—Deceased died of acute peritonitis resulting from 2 cm gastric perforation caused by severe blunt force trauma to the abdomen—Whether prosecution established prima facie case at close of prosecution’s case and proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt at close of defense's case—Objective-subjective test under s 300(c) of the Penal Code—Whether the accused intentionally inflicted bodily injury and whether the injury intended was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death—Whether absence of premeditation or prior planning negated murder—Whether facts fell within culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s 304(a) or s 304(b) of the Penal Code—Penal Code ss 300(c), 302, 304(a), and 304(b) Criminal Procedure—Charge—Particulars of time—Variance between time stated in charge and medical evidence—Charge sheet specified offence occurred between 5.40 pm and 7.00 pm on 21 April 2022—Histological dating placed fatal blunt force abdominal trauma approximately one day earlier when the accused had exclusive custody—Whether failure to amend charge under s 158 of the Criminal Procedure Code rendered charge defective—Whether timeframe stated in charge construed as culmination of continuous fatal transaction ending in collapse and death—Whether variance cured under ss 156 and 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code where the accused was not misled and no failure of justice was occasioned—Criminal Procedure Code ss 152, 153, 156, 158, and 422 Criminal Procedure—Defence—Alibi—Notice of alibi—Accused claimed presence with deceased’s mother at Ramadan bazaar during charged timeframe on 21 April 2022—Failure to serve mandatory written notice of alibi under s 402A of the Criminal Procedure Code—Whether informal alibi failed procedurally and substantively where accused admitted sole custody prior to bazaar outing and medical pathology established progressive peritonitis developing over hours—Criminal Procedure Code s 402A Criminal Procedure—Sentence—Murder of child—Abolition of Mandatory Death Penalty Act 2023—Statutory discretion under amended s 302 of the Penal Code—Whether death penalty reserved for exceptional and most heinous cases—Balancing mitigating factors of accused’s youth and lack of prior convictions against aggravating cruelty inflicted on defenceless toddler in stepfather’s trust—Imposition of 35 years’ imprisonment from date of arrest and whipping of 15 strokes—Penal Code s 302 Criminal Procedure—Trial—Close of prosecution’s case and close of defense's case—Maximum evaluation under s 180 of the Criminal Procedure Code—Fresh judgments.title: TENAGA PTARAS (M) SDN BHD v TELEKOM MALAYSIA BERHAD & ors
judgments.catchwords: Catchwords An appeal filed by the Appellant - (the Third Party in the court below), against my decision delivered on 28 August 2026. I dismissed the Third Party’s appeal application which is an appeal on the entire decision of the learned Sessions Court Judge of Kuala Lumpur dated 18 September 2025 with costs - The Sessions Court Judge (SCJ) had allowed the First Respondent's (“the Plaintiff”) claim for damages in the sum of RM715,722.80 with costs of RM10,000.00 against the Second Respondent (“the Defendant”) - Concurrently, the SCJ allowed the Defendant’s claim against the Third Party for a full indemnity in respect of the Plaintiff's claim, along with costs of RM10,000.00 - The dispute in which the Third Party, as subcontractor, sued the Defendant for outstanding contractual payments - The Third Party was appointed by the Defendant on 22 April 2019 as its subcontractor for one Project - On 20 March 2019, the Plaintiff received complaints of an abrupt telecommunication service disruption in the Kampung Baru Sungai Buloh area. Upon immediate physical inspection and technical testing - the Plaintiff discovered damage to its underground cable and ducts located in front of a shop Kedai Galas Bebola (Bearing) at Jalan Welfare, Kampung Baru Sungai Buloh, approximately 4.05 km from the Plaintiff’s Sungai Buloh Exchange - the Plaintiff's technical personnel from the External Network Zone conducted patrols and technical testing, which confirmed that the point of cable damage corresponded with the Site where newly laid pavement was observed - On 11 April 2019, the Plaintiff lodged a police report of the cable fault occurred at the Site - It was undisputed that the Defendant, had been appointed by TNB as the main contractor under Tender Pukal KLB2351 to carry out excavation, trenching, and cable-laying works in that exact alignment along Jalan Welfare. The Defendant, in turn, appointed the Third Party as its subcontractor to carry out the physical excavation and cable installation works via a Letter of Award dated 22 April 2019 - The Plaintiff undertook emergency rectification and reinstatement works, appointed the contractors to carry out repair works on the Plaintiff’s cable fault caused by the Defendant - On 15 April 2019, the Plaintiff formally notified the Defendant of the damage and requested them to contact their insurer - MSIG Insurance declines the Defendant's insurance claim stating that the adjuster's investigation confirmed that Third Party caused the damage, but coverage is voided due to their failure to conduct underground utility mapping - the Plaintiff received the Defendant’s reply letter whereby the Defendant did not deny the Plaintiff’s claim and informed that the Defendant is in the process of claiming from its insurance - the Defendant claims that the works was carried out by the Third Party based on the police report of 6 December 2019 and the investigation carried out by the insurer MSIG which revealed that the Third Party carried out the excavation works at the project site - After the full trial, the SCJ decided that the burden of proof is on the Plaintiff to proof negligence as in its paragraphs 18 -19 of the SCJ’s ground of judgment. The SCJ held that the Defendant had a duty of care to ensure that its excavation works did not damage the underground telecommunication utilities. This duty was breached when excavation was conducted without a proper underground utility mapping. Relying upon the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur and the contemporaneous conduct of the parties, specifically the Defendant's failure to deny liability, their insurance claims, and the Third Party’s supervisor's police report admitting presence on 20 March 2019, the SCJ held that the Defendant is liable in negligence - With regard to the third-party proceedings, the SCJ found that the Third Party was the actual tortfeasor that carried out the physical excavation on site and directly severed th

judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

judgments.title: ROSLI A/L JENDUT & ors v AGROBEST (M) SDN. BHD & ors
judgments.catchwords: Notice of Appeal filed by defendants against the whole of the High Court’s decision eventhough the dismissal of the plaintiffs’ claim for special and exemplary damages were in defendants favour — whether plaintiffs ought to have filed a Notice of Appeal if they had wanted to appeal against the dismissal of their claim for special and exemplary damages —-Rules 5,8, 1A, 102, 103, 104, 105 Rules of Court of Appeal 1994 (RCA 1994), s 69(5) Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (CJA) —Proof of the Indigenous People of their connection to the deceased persons’ tombstones and grave sites — use of oral tradition and narratives under s 32(1)(d) and (e) Evidence Act 1950 (EA) — locus of the plaintiffs to sue for trespass for the demolition and desecration of their ancestors’ tombstones and grave sites —- nature of customary title — whether it has been extinguished before the alienation and issuance of land titles to private corporations —- effect of a 4(2)(a) National Land Code (NLC) on the law for the time being in force on customary tenure — whether Article 5(1) on right to life covers the protection of the indigenous peoples’ burial sites, custom and tradition —United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) and its use in interpreting Constitutional Rights.
